topic_title: Related Parties on the Committee of Creditors: Why Some Financial Creditors Don't Get a Vote Under IBC Section 21(2)
angle: A guide for financial creditors, resolution professionals and corporate debtors on how the Section 21(2) proviso excludes related-party financial creditors from CoC representation, participation and voting, and the narrow statutory exception that lets some of them back in.
key_points: The proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC bars a financial creditor that is a 'related party' of the corporate debtor (as defined in Section 5(24)) from any right of representation, participation or voting in CoC meetings

Related-party status for this purpose can arise from equity/voting control, common directorship or management, or other relationships listed in Section 5(24), and courts have read the exclusion purposively to catch disguised or collusive related-party financing used to influence CoC outcomes

A second proviso carves out an exception: a financial creditor regulated by a financial sector regulator is not excluded merely because it became a related party solely through conversion of debt into equity (or instruments convertible into equity) before the insolvency commencement date

The test for exclusion looks at the relationship existing as of the insolvency commencement date in most judicial readings, with courts scrutinising last-minute restructurings designed to artificially gain or escape related-party status

A resolution professional who wrongly admits a related party to CoC voting (or wrongly excludes a genuine arm's-length creditor as related) exposes the CoC's decisions, including plan approval, to challenge before the NCLT/NCLAT

Practical steps for creditors and RPs: documenting the actual ownership/control chain and transaction history behind any financial debt claim, and flagging related-party questions early rather than after a contested CoC vote
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: the proviso to Section 21(2) of the IBC excludes a related-party financial creditor from CoC representation, participation and voting, with 'related party' defined in Section 5(24)
confirmed: a second proviso exempts financial-sector-regulated creditors that became related parties solely through pre-insolvency debt-to-equity conversion
confirmed: courts (including the Supreme Court) have applied a purposive interpretation to prevent related parties from being included in or manipulating the CoC through collusive transactions

topic_title: When Can a Plaint Be Rejected Under Order VII Rule 11 CPC? A Practical Guide
angle: A guide for both plaintiffs and defendants in civil and commercial suits on the narrow, plaint-averments-only test courts apply when a defendant seeks early rejection of a suit under Order VII Rule 11, and when such an application will (and won't) succeed.
key_points: Order VII Rule 11 CPC lists specific grounds for rejecting a plaint at the threshold: no disclosed cause of action, undervaluation of relief, insufficient stamping, the suit being barred by law, failure to file in duplicate, and non-compliance with Order VII Rule 9 on documents

Courts decide such an application by looking only at the averments in the plaint itself (and documents filed with it) -- the defendant's written statement, defence or external evidence cannot be relied on to reject a plaint

No evidence or merits of the underlying controversy can be examined at this stage; the court must assume the plaint's factual averments are true for the limited purpose of deciding whether a cause of action or a legal bar is disclosed on the face of the plaint

Where limitation or another legal bar is obvious and glaring from the plaint's own averments, courts have held they should reject the plaint at the threshold rather than let a hopeless suit proceed to trial
If a plaint claims several reliefs and at least one is properly pleaded and maintainable, the entire plaint cannot be rejected merely because other reliefs may not be maintainable

Strategic use: a well-prepared Order VII Rule 11 application can end a suit at an early, inexpensive stage, but a plaintiff can often defeat it by ensuring the plaint itself pleads enough facts to disclose a cause of action and to show the claim isn't ex facie time-barred
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Order VII Rule 11(a)-(f) CPC sets out the six specific grounds for rejection of a plaint

confirmed: Supreme Court has repeatedly held that only the plaint's own averments (not the defence or external evidence) are considered on an Order VII Rule 11 application, and that evidence/merits cannot be examined at that stage

confirmed: Supreme Court has held a plaint can be rejected at the threshold where the limitation bar is obvious from the pleadings, and that partial rejection is not permitted where at least one pleaded relief is maintainable

topic_title: Is Minimum Support Price (MSP) Legally Enforceable? What Farmers Can and Cannot Claim in Court
angle: A guide for farmers, FPOs and agri-businesses on the actual legal status of MSP in India -- a policy announcement rather than a statutory entitlement -- what limited remedies currently exist, and the pending litigation seeking to make it a legal right.
key_points: MSP is announced by the Government on the recommendation of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) as a policy/administrative price-support mechanism; it has no dedicated statute making it a legally enforceable right, and government procurement agencies are not under a statutory obligation to buy every farmer's produce at MSP

A farmer cannot, as matters currently stand, sue to compel payment of MSP for produce sold in the open market to a private buyer below the announced MSP, since there is no law mandating private buyers pay MSP or making the floor price legally binding

Where the government or a designated procurement agency (e.g., for paddy, wheat, cotton) does operate a procurement scheme, farmers can seek remedies tied to that specific scheme's procurement guidelines (e.g., unjustified rejection on quality grounds, procurement centre access) rather than a freestanding 'right to MSP'

A batch of petitions is pending before the Supreme Court seeking a legally guaranteed MSP for all notified crops computed on a cost-of-cultivation-plus-50%-profit (C2+50%) formula based on the Swaminathan Commission Report, with the Court seeking the Centre's response -- this remains unresolved and should be tracked rather than treated as settled law

Separately, the Essential Commodities Act and state APMC/agricultural produce marketing laws regulate where and how produce can be sold and what licensing traders need, which is distinct from and does not itself guarantee a floor price

Practical guidance for farmers and FPOs: document produce quality and procurement-centre interactions carefully when relying on a government scheme, since remedies currently run through the specific scheme's own grievance mechanism rather than a general MSP enforcement right
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: there is no central statute making MSP a legally enforceable right; MSP is fixed by government policy on CACP's recommendation and procurement is scheme-based

confirmed: a plea seeking a legally guaranteed MSP based on the Swaminathan Commission's C2+50% formula is pending before the Supreme Court, which has sought a response from the Centre -- this is an open/unresolved matter, not decided law
varies: specific procurement scheme guidelines, grievance mechanisms and which crops have active government procurement vary by state and by crop season

topic_title: Benami Transactions: How Attachment and Confiscation Actually Work Under the 2016 Amendment Act
angle: A guide for property owners, family members on a property title, and anyone structuring a purchase in another's name, explaining the enforcement machinery under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016 and the real risk of losing the property without compensation.
key_points: The Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016, in force from 1 November 2016, substantially overhauled the original 1988 Act, defining 'benami transaction' and creating a dedicated enforcement machinery: an Initiating Officer, an Approving Authority, an Adjudicating Authority, and an Appellate Tribunal

Under Section 24, the Initiating Officer who has reason to believe a person holds benami property issues notice to both the benamidar (the name-holder) and the beneficial owner, where known, and may provisionally attach the property (with Approving Authority approval) for up to 90 days to prevent it being alienated during the inquiry

Within 15 days of a provisional attachment order, the Initiating Officer must refer the matter to the Adjudicating Authority, which decides, after hearing the affected persons, whether to confirm the attachment

Where the Adjudicating Authority ultimately confirms the property is benami, it passes a confiscation order; on confiscation, all rights and title vest absolutely in the Central Government free of encumbrances, and no compensation is payable

The Act also carries criminal exposure -- rigorous imprisonment and a fine -- for entering into a benami transaction to defeat the law or evade creditors or statutory dues, separate from the confiscation proceedings against the property itself

Common exceptions preserved under the Act include property held by a person in a fiduciary capacity, and property purchased in the name of a spouse or unmarried daughter for which consideration is traceable to known sources of the person providing it -- though these exceptions are narrowly construed and fact-dependent
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016 in force from 1 November 2016, establishing the Initiating Officer/Adjudicating Authority/Appellate Tribunal structure
confirmed: Section 24 provisional attachment (up to 90 days) and the 15-day reference requirement to the Adjudicating Authority
confirmed: confiscation under a confirmed order vests the property in the Central Government free of encumbrances with no compensation payable

topic_title: Challenging an Environmental Clearance at the NGT: The Section 16 Appeal Process and Its Tight Deadlines
angle: A guide for a project proponent defending a granted EC, or a community/objector challenging one, on how an environmental clearance appeal actually works before the National Green Tribunal and why missing the limitation window is usually fatal.
key_points: An order granting or refusing environmental clearance can be appealed to the National Green Tribunal under Section 16(h) of the NGT Act, 2010, and the appeal can be filed by any person aggrieved, including on environmental-interest grounds, not only a direct commercial rival

The limitation period is a strict 30 days from the date the EC order is communicated or otherwise made known to the appellant, calculated from the earliest date of effective public disclosure (such as upload on the relevant authority's website)
The NGT has power to condone a further delay of up to 60 days on sufficient cause being shown, making 90 days the absolute outer limit

Following an NGT Principal Bench practice direction, appeals filed beyond the 90-day outer limit are virtually always dismissed as time-barred, regardless of the merits of the environmental objections raised

Because the clock runs from disclosure rather than actual knowledge, a project proponent should ensure proper, timely publication of the EC to start and close the limitation window, while an intending objector must monitor clearance portals proactively rather than waiting for formal personal notice

On a successful appeal, the NGT can modify conditions, remand for fresh consideration by the authority, or quash the clearance outright, with significant practical consequences for a project already underway
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Section 16(h) of the NGT Act, 2010 provides the right of appeal against an order granting or refusing environmental clearance

confirmed: 30-day limitation period from communication, condonable by a further 60 days (90-day outer limit), as applied via NGT Principal Bench practice (order dated 12 August 2024) under which appeals beyond 90 days are virtually always dismissed
confirmed: limitation runs from the earliest date of effective communication/public disclosure of the EC order, not from a party's actual subjective knowledge

topic_title: Invoking a Pledge of Shares: What a Lender Can (and Can't) Do on Borrower Default
angle: A guide for lenders and promoters on how a share pledge -- a common security structure in promoter-financing and acquisition-finance deals -- is actually invoked on default, distinct from the site's existing personal-guarantee and bank-guarantee content.
key_points: A pledge of shares as loan security is governed by a combination of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (pledge/bailment provisions), the Companies Act, 2013 (charge registration), the Depositories Act, 1996 and SEBI's depository regulations, and, where applicable, the SARFAESI Act, 2002
Under the Companies Act, 2013, a company creating a pledge over its shares is required to have the charge registered, and an unregistered charge cannot be enforced against the company by a creditor

On default, a pledgee-lender's core contract-law options are to sue for recovery while retaining the pledge as security, or to sell the pledged shares after giving the borrower reasonable notice of the intended sale

On proper invocation, a pledgee (or its assignee) can get itself registered as beneficial owner of the dematerialised pledged shares, entitling it to exercise voting and other shareholder rights attached to those shares -- a point affirmed by Bombay High Court authority

The pledgor's right of redemption survives invocation and registration as beneficial owner -- it is only extinguished once the shares are actually sold to a third party, so a borrower retains a window to redeem by clearing the debt even after the pledge is invoked

Practical lender diligence: confirming the charge is duly registered, that depository/DP-level invocation formalities are correctly followed, and that notice requirements are satisfied before relying on invoked pledged shares as the primary recovery route
facts_to_verify_or_confirmed: confirmed: Companies Act, 2013 charge-registration requirement applies to a pledge of a company's shares, and an unregistered charge is unenforceable against the company
confirmed: Bombay High Court authority affirms a pledgee/assignee's right to be registered as beneficial owner of invoked dematerialised pledged shares and to exercise voting rights as such
confirmed: the pledgor's right of redemption continues until actual sale of the shares to a third party, under general pledge/bailment principles
